svg.title: Cells & fuel cells
svg.desc: Simple cells: Two different metals in electrolyte, connected externally. Chemical reaction supplies electrical energy. Voltage depends on electrodes and electrolyte. Keep electrolyte/concentration and temperature fixed when comparing metals. Use lead polarity and reference convention to interpret reactivity data. Batteries & recharge: Series voltages add: 3 × 1.5 V = 4.5 V. Battery = two or more cells. Non-rechargeable, e.g. alkaline: stops when reactant is used up. Rechargeable: external current reverses chemical reactions. Compare mass, capacity, lifetime cost and recharge time. Continuous fuel supply: External hydrogen and oxygen/air feed the cell. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Hydrogen oxidised; oxygen reduced. Electrons travel through external circuit/load; ions through electrolyte. Continues while supplied with reactants; refill fuel rather than reverse reaction to recharge. Acidic half-equations: Hydrogen: 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. Oxygen: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O. Add and cancel H⁺/electrons. Balance atoms and charge. Fuel cell generates current; electrolysis requires a power supply. If electrolyte is alkaline: Hydrogen: 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻. Oxygen: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Sum gives same overall reaction. Use the electrolyte specified; do not mix acidic and alkaline half-equations. Fuel cell vs rechargeable: Fuel: water during use, quick refuelling possible; hydrogen storage, flammability and infrastructure matter. Battery: recharge from grid, no exhaust; mass, charge time, finite life and materials matter. Check hydrogen production/electricity sources, efficiency and manufacture. Neither is automatically zero-carbon overall.
